**MTN Group Limited** (formerly **M-Cell**)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-2) is a [South African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa")[multinational corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation") and mobile [telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunications "Telecommunications") provider. Its head office is in [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-4) MTN is among the [largest mobile network operators in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mobile_network_operators "List of mobile network operators"), and the largest in [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa").

In October 2025, MTN announced it had surpassed 300 million customers, the first African-headquartered telco to reach that milestone, making it the sixth-largest in the world by subscriber count. It has a footprint in sixteen countries in Africa and the Middle East.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The company was founded in 1994 as M-Cell with assistance from the South African government.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-8) In 1995, it replaced its then CEO, John Beck, with Robert (Bob) Chaphe and founder Leena Jaitley.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-9) In 2001, the company reported that its controlling shareholder was Johnnic Holdings, and the chairperson was [Irene Charnley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_Charnley "Irene Charnley").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-10) In 2002, [Phuthuma Nhleko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phuthuma_Nhleko "Phuthuma Nhleko") became the CEO,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-11) replacing then-CEO Paul Edwards, who had invested in expansion to Nigeria.[[12]](

M-Net (an abbreviation of Electronic Media Network) is a South African pay television channel established by Naspers in 1986.[1] The channel broadcasts both local and international programming, including general entertainment, children's series, sport and movies. While the TV signal is generally encrypted, M-Net showed some programmes 'free to air' in its "Open Time" slot between 5 p.m. and 7 pm, until the slot closed on 1 April 2007.

In the early 1990s, M-Net added a second analogue channel called Community Services Network (CSN),[2] and began digital broadcasting via satellite to the rest of Africa, via its sister company MultiChoice (now owned by Canal+ S.A.). With the introduction of MultiChoice's multi-channel digital satellite TV service, DStv, in 1995, several different channels have been created to complement the original M-Net channel, including the now-defunct M-Net Series and several film/movie channels based on genre and preference.

The channel also had a separate terrestrial feed which, in 2011, still had composite programming from kykNET and SuperSport. Its legacy subscriber base was moved to DStv or GOtv when the analogue terrestrial service was switched off.

Historyedit
	
This section needs more citations. Please help improve this section by adding citations to reliable sources. Unsourced material may be challenged and removed. (September 2014) (Learn how and when to remove this message)
1980sedit

The idea of a pay-TV network in South Africa came to life as early as 1982, when Nasionale Pers (Naspers) – headed by executive Koos Bekker — started to promote the idea to the country's other three largest media corporations: Times Media Ltd (now Avusa/BDFM), Argus (now the Independent Group) and Perskor (which is now defunct).[3]

The initial project by Ton Vosloo in 1982 suggested that the new channel would restore the revenue of its newspapers.[4]

The newspapers and magazines published by Naspers had lost a lot of advertising revenue to the SABC after the arrival of television and for this reason, according to some sources, the National Party government wanted Naspers to run its own television network.[3]

Initially, the plan was for M-Net to be jointly owned by the four media corporations, with the Natal Witness also having a small share in the station. However, as time went on, the project became that of Naspers only.

On 27 November 1984, Foreign Affairs minister Pik Botha suggested the creation of a feasibility study for the subscription network, assisted by a working group.[4] On 25 April 1985, the press consortium won the bid, over 39 other applicants. Naspers would hold 26%, the three other groups 23% each and the two independent newspapers 5% each. The new service would have a set of guidelines: no news or political coverage, no exclusive sports screenings, no more than nine hours on air per day and no advertising. The format would emulate that of SABC's TV4, which ran on its black networks (TV2 and TV3) from 9pm to closedown.[4]

In October 1986, they started broadcasting for 12 hours a day – initially to Johannesburg and Pretoria, to about 500 households who had bought decoders.[5] Their aim at that stage was to sell 9,000 decoders per month.[3] The service used the Oak Orion scrambling system, and the decoders were manufactured in South Africa by the local affiliate of Matsushita Electric.[6] That small start finally broke the TV monopoly by SABC.

Although it was subscription-based, the Broadcasting Authority granted them a one-hour time slot each day, in which the channel could broadcast unencrypted, free-to-air content, in order to promote itself and attract potential subscribers. In 1987, the Cabinet also approved an arrangement under which the SABC was required to make its TV4 channel available to M-Net between 6 and 7pm.[7] This time slot became known as Open Time; though it was only meant to be temporary — M-Net was supposed to close Open Time immediately when it had 150,000 subscribers – it remained.[8]

At the end of its first year, they recorded a loss of R37 million.[3] However, it pushed forward and eventually, the public started taking notice. After two years, the loss was turned into a R20 million profit.[3] In 1988, the channel launched Carte Blanche, a multi-award-winning actuality program hosted by Derek Watts and Ruda Landman. In only a few years, Carte Blanche became famous for its investigative journalism. In the process, the show also uncovered many of South Africa's most famous scandals of human rights abuse, corruption and consumer affairs.

1989 saw the launch of M-Net SuperSport, which went on to become South Africa's (and Sub-Saharan Africa's) first dedicated sports channel which spawned into sports-specific channels from 2003 onward. It was the year they adopted a new slogan – We Won't Stop the Magic, backed by a massive ad campaign.

1990sedit

1990 was the first year that they made a profit[9] and also the year that saw a few major changes for the channel. It launched K-TV, a daily time slot specialising in kids' entertainment, and in July 1991[10] Open Time was expanded from the initial one hour per day, to two. They applied for a licence to broadcast news and the application was granted in December 1990. (Former State President P.W. Botha once claimed that "M-Net would not broadcast news as long as he was State President."[11]) but during June 1991, they announced that they were putting their plans for news broadcasts aside and that, instead, more money would be invested in local productions, including South Africa's first local soap opera Egoli, which started on 6 April 1992 and ended on 31 March 2010. However, they began re-broadcasting BBC World Service Television (now BBC World News) that same year. In addition to news, the channel started airing sporting events, per a January 1991 amendment.[4]

In early 1994, M-Net started broadcasting to Nigeria in Lagos.[12] By 1995, the channel was also being carried in Uganda over VHF, Namibia over VHF and Lesotho using Lesotho Television's network.[13]

M-Net SuperSport changed its name in 1994 to SuperSport only, to create a more recognizable brand. During that year it broadcast live coverage of South Africa's test cricket series in Australia for the first time. At the same time, Hugh Bladen and Naas Botha – two of the channel's most colourful rugby commentators — joined SuperSport. By that time, its sports coverage became very impressive, including the US Masters, the FA Cup Finals, the Indy 500, the US PGA Championship, Wimbledon, the Tour de France, MotoGP and an ever-expanding rugby package. In 1995, SuperSport started broadcasting 24 hours per day on M-Net's spare channel, the Community Service Network, which paved the way for a 24-hour multi-channel sports network. When rugby became a full professional sport in 1995, most of the broadcasting rights in the Southern Hemisphere were sold to Rupert Murdoch's News Corporation. In response, they started negotiating with NewsCorp in August 1995 and in February the following year, SuperSport was granted sole broadcasting rights to both the Super 12 and Tri Nations rugby tournaments.[14] It was a major breakthrough for the channel as well as SuperSport, which had by then expanded to sports-and-leagues-specific TV channels on DStv and GOtv, MultiChoice's satellite TV services.

As of 1999, M-Net was one of the three television networks in the world to have agreements with every major American film studio, having signed a contract with Warner Bros., in an exclusive deal that was snatched from upstart terrestrial broadcaster e.tv. Its content would appear on its channels effective 1 April 1999.[15] On 1 November that year, M-Net expanded its Open Time slot to other African countries where the channel was relayed on terrestrial television.[16]

2000sedit

The channel rebranded again on 11 February 2001 with the new tagline "We Call it Magic". The new logo incorporated the iconic M symbol inside a square, representing the values of M-Net as a "brave, colourful and exciting channel", while also accommodating it with its sub-brands, and strengthening its ties with the wider network of M-Net sister channels. In addition, M-Net had secured the rights to the American reality show Temptation Island, shot in Belize.[17] The network also secured the rights to the smash hit reality format Big Brother, with the aim of producing a localised version for South Africa. The first season alone was set to be the biggest production to date, with a record-breaking number of 120 jobs, the equivalent of three separate productions, created in its making.[18] M-Net had plans to continue its growth strategy in 2002.[19] Following on from the success of Big Brother, the channel secured the rights to another groundbreaking international format, Idols, which premiered on 10 March 2002.[20]

ICASA ruled in favour of the withdrawal of Open Time on its terrestrial feed on 1 June 2005, seeing it as unfair for a subscription-based network. The new rule was put into effect from 1 April 2007.[21] Ahead of closing, some 550,000 South Africans regularly watched the slot, which consisted largely of local productions. To deal with its loss of revenue, projected to be at R60 million, M-Net unveiled a one-hour block of its original soaps (among them Egoli) from April 2007.[22]

2010sedit

A new line-up was introduced on 1 April 2011, which implied the end of Afrikaans and sports programming on the satellite feed of the channel, as well as the removal of KTV from both terrestrial and satellite feeds. KTV was removed because the target audience migrated to DSTV's dedicated kids channels, while the sports and Afrikaans programming continued on the terrestrial feed because its subscribers did not have sports and language-specific channels. With these changes, the satellite feed would only air English-language entertainment programming all day.[23] On 21 February 2018, Multichoice announced the shutdown of the terrestrial feed with the switch-off of its analogue subscription network, with the migration completing on 31 March. After the shutdown date, its legacy analogue subscribers went to either DStv (in areas without DTT signal) or GOtv.[24]

High definitionedit

Delivery of high-definition content started with the launch of DStv's first high definition decoder the HD PVR, XtraView and the first HD channel, M-Net HD. M-Net began broadcasting a 720p high definition channel in 2010, which is available for HD-PVR subscribers; the standard definition channel for non-HD-PVR subscribers is merely downscaled at the provider from the HD feed rather than having a devoted analog channel. In 2012, the original film/movie channels were expanded to 6 channels which grouped films according to genre/preference.[25]

M-Net channelsedit
M-Netedit

The original M-Net channel broadcasts general entertainment, as well as premiere movies, documentaries, music specials and first-run TV series. The channel has a timeshift service, a terrestrial service and a CSN in South Africa. In other African countries the channel broadcasts exclusively on the DStv Service with two different feeds, M-Net East for East Africa and M-Net West for West Africa. These feeds broadcasts nearly the same content, though the West African feed is 2 hours ahead of the East African feed as programmes are scheduled based on the local time zones of the regions (EAT and WAT respectively) except for some live programmes. Advertising on the East feed is targeted at Kenyan viewers while the West feed is targeted at Nigerian Viewers. Over the course of several years, M-Net has launched numerous sister channels. In DStv, the channel is only available to the high tier package Premium as it contains expensive content.

M-Net Edge

On 31 March 2017, M-Net Edge programs were moved to M-Net as part of a merge and various other channels from M-Net.

M-Net +1

The time shift channel, M-Net +1 was launched also for DStv Premium customers since 1 June 2016 on DStv channel 901.[26] However, the time-shifted channel was discontinued on 16 May 2021 due to increase of content preference by DStv Premium Subscribers on the DStv app.[27][28]

M-Net Moviesedit
Main article: M-Net Movies

The original two movie channels, Movie Magic 1 and Movie Magic 2, launched in 1995 to coincide with the launch of DStv, were renamed M-Net Movies 1 and M-Net Movies 2, respectively, in 2005. Two additional movie channels, M-Net Movies Stars (previously M-Net Stars which launched in 2009) and actionX (which was renamed M-Net Action in 2008), were later launched. In October 2012, the channels were expanded to six which grouped films according to genre and preference. The 7 film/movie channels were later reconsolidated into 4 numeric channels.

In August 2026, it was announced that M-Net Movies 1 would be merged with M-Net Movies 2 to become M Movies+, M-Net Movies 3 becomes M Movies Stars and M-Net Movies 4 becomes M Movies Legends.[29]

1Magic and Meedit
Main articles: 1Magic and Me (TV channel)

Most of the programmes broadcast are unique to M-Net Series but some are rebroadcasts of episodes previously shown on M-Net.

A single series channel known as The Series Channel (renamed as M-Net Series in 2005) was introduced in April 1998 as a sister channel to the original M-Net channel. On 9 July 2013, this channel was split into three, namely:

M-Net Series Showcase, which was broadcast in high definition, previously served as the primary series channel on which most new content unique to Series was broadcast.
M-Net Series Reality broadcast talk shows and other reality media.
M-Net Series Zone which served as a catch-up channel, and featured previous seasons of shows. Several TV shows also ran back-to-back in marathon blocks.

On 11 September 2014, it was announced that Showcase and Reality would be discontinued and replaced with two new channels, VUZU Amp and M-Net Edge, on 20 and 13 October, respectively.[30] Only one channel of the original three, M-Net Series Zone, remained. The standalone channel is reminiscent of the initial channel, in that it airs shows that previously aired on the main M-Net channel. It was rebranded M-Net City in 2015. On 29 January 2018, VUZU Amp was rebranded as 1Magic.

M-Net City, along with VUZU, was closed on 29 October 2021 to be replaced by ME on its EPG slot. Both channels went dark on the platform by 2 February 2024.

kykNETedit
Main article: kykNET

kykNET, which broadcasts solely in Afrikaans, was launched in October 1999. The channel features general entertainment, series, informative programs and music. kykNET also has two sister channels, kykNET & Kie and kykNET Musiek (now known as kykNET Nou!).[31] DStv announced on 16 July 2014 that kykNET would be broadcast in high definition as of 12 August 2014.[32]

It was launched in the UK on TalkTalk's IPTV service, TalkTalk Plus TV, in October 2013.[33] However, it was dropped by TalkTalk in December 2015.[34] A kykNET International service was available online to subscribers in selected countries in North America, Europe and Australasia via the Showmax platform.[35]

VUZUedit

VUZU, originally launched as Go in 2003, had a strong focus on Southern African youth, specifically preteens, teens and the 20–49 demographics, similar to some popular American television channels such as Bravo, FX, BET, The CW, NBC, TNT and many others. A sister channel, VUZU Amp, was launched in October 2014, which was later relaunched as 1Magic.

The channel was shut down, along with M-Net City, on 29 October 2021 to be replaced by Me.

Mzansi Magicedit

Mzansi Magic features original South African series, movies, music, documentaries and reality shows. It has two sister channels, Mzansi Magic Music, Mzansi Wethu and Mzansi Biskop.

Africa Magicedit

Africa Magic, which started off as a single channel of the same name, is a brand owned by M-Net and MultiChoice and now comprises 7 channels. The first Africa Magic channel was launched in July 2003 as a movie channel and over the next decade, the brand expanded to include 6 more channels comprising movies, television shows and general entertainment. Africa Magic currently broadcasts in more than 50 African countries. The channels include Africa Magic Family, Africa Magic Showcase, Africa Magic Yoruba, Africa Magic Igbo, Africa Magic Hausa. Africa Magic Epic and Africa Magic Urban. Africa Magic is also responsible for the annual Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards (AMVCAs), the biggest celebration of film and television talent in Africa.

Maisha Magicedit

Maisha Magic comprises four channels, Maisha Magic East & Maisha Magic Plus for Kenyan audiences and Maisha Magic Bongo & Maisha Magic Poa for Tanzanian audiences. They focus on East African movies, series and music. It was initially launched as Africa Magic Swahili but was later rebranded as Maisha Magic before it became Maisha Magic Swahili then rebranded again as Maisha Magic East. Maisha Magic Bongo have been working with many producers from Tanzania like Mtitu Game 1st Quality, Steps Entertainment, Halisi Film, Joh Films, Severini Film Entertainment, 360 Production etc.

In 2021, the brand introduced Maisha Magic Movies showcasing the best Ugandan, Kenyan and Tanzanian movies.

Channel Oedit

Channel O is a present music channel with a strong focus on urban music genres. It also holds the annual Channel O Music Video Awards ceremony where artists are awarded for their outstanding contribution to music.

SuperSportedit

SuperSport is a group of sport television channels carried on DStv and GOtv. It provides sports content in South Africa and many other African countries.

**Naspers Limited** (formerly **Die Nasionale Pers**) is a South African [multinational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation"), [internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_service_provider "Online service provider"), [technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_company "Technology company") and multimedia [holding company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holding_company "Holding company")[headquartered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headquarters "Headquarters") in [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town").

The company has interests in online retail, publishing, [real estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate"), and [venture capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital "Venture capital")[investment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment "Investment"). Naspers' principal shareholder is its [Dutch-listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euronext_Amsterdam "Euronext Amsterdam") investment subsidiary, [Prosus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosus "Prosus"), which owns approximately 49% of its parent as part of a [cross-ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_ownership "Cross ownership") structure.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naspers#cite_note-news24-5)

Founded in 1915 by attorney [William Angus Hofmeyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Angus_Hofmeyr?action=edit&redlink=1 "William Angus Hofmeyr (page does not exist)")[[af](https://af.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie%20Hofmeyr "af:Willie Hofmeyr")], Die Nasionale Pers was the largest publishing company in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") throughout the 20th century with interests across newspapers, magazines and books. In the 1980s, the company began to diversify, launching a subscription television service and investing in markets outside of South Africa for the first time.

In 2001, Naspers made an early investment in Chinese technology firm [Tencent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tencent "Tencent") and became increasingly focused on the global consumer internet sector. In 2019, Naspers listed its global internet investment business unit Prosus (including a 31% stake in Tencent) on Euronext Amsterdam.

As of 2021, Naspers owned a 56.92% stake in Prosus[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naspers#cite_note-news24-5) and wholly owns [Media24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media24 "Media24") (Africa's largest publishing company), [Takealot.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takealot.com "Takealot.com") (South Africa's largest online retailer) and Naspers Foundry, a South African focused venture capital fund.

Barbados[a] is an island nation in the Caribbean Sea. It is part of the Lesser Antilles of the West Indies and is the southernmost and easternmost island of the Caribbean region. It lies on the boundary of the South American and Caribbean tectonic plates. Its capital and largest city is Bridgetown.

Inhabited by Kalinago people since the 13th century, and prior to that by other Indigenous peoples, the island was originally named Ichirouganaim.[7] It was claimed for the Crown of Castile by Spanish navigators in the late 15th century, who named it Barbudos, and it first appeared on a Spanish map in 1511.[8] The Portuguese Empire claimed the island between 1532 and 1536, but abandoned it in 1620; their only traces were the introduction of wild boars intended as a supply of meat whenever the island was visited. The indigenous population had mostly been sold into slavery, killed, or died of disease by that time.[7]

An English ship, the Olive Blossom, arrived in Barbados on 14 May 1625; its men took possession of the island in the name of King James I. In 1627, the first permanent settlers arrived from England, and Barbados became an English and later British colony.[9] During this period, the colony operated on a plantation economy, relying initially on the labour of Irish indentured servants[10] and subsequently African slaves, who worked on the island's plantations. Slavery continued until it was phased out through most of the British Empire by the Slavery Abolition Act 1833. The descendants of these enslaved Africans now account for over 90% of the island's population.[11]

On 30 November 1966, Barbados moved toward political independence and assumed the status of a Commonwealth realm, becoming a sovereign state with Elizabeth II as Queen of Barbados. On 30 November 2021, Barbados transitioned to a republic within the Commonwealth, replacing its monarchy with a ceremonial president.[12][13]

Barbados is ranked as one of the Caribbean's leading tourist destinations.[14]

Etymologyedit

The name "Barbados" is from either the Portuguese term os barbados or the Spanish equivalent, los barbados, both meaning "the bearded ones".[15][16] Whether "bearded" refers to the long, hanging roots of the bearded fig tree (Ficus citrifolia), a species of banyan indigenous to the island, or to the allegedly bearded Kalinago (Island Caribs) who once inhabited the island, or, more fancifully, to a visual impression of a beard formed by the sea foam that sprays over the outlying coral reefs is unclear. In 1519, a map produced by Genoese mapmaker Visconte Maggiolo showed and named Barbados in its correct position.[17] Furthermore, the island of Barbuda in the Leewards is very similar in name and was once named "Las Barbudas" by the Spanish.[citation needed]

The original name for Barbados in the pre-Columbian era was Ichirouganaim, according to accounts by descendants of the Indigenous Arawakan-speaking tribes in other regional areas, with possible translations including "Red land with white teeth"[18] or "Redstone island with teeth outside (reefs)"[19] or simply "Teeth".[20][21][22]

Colloquially, Barbadians refer to their home island as "Bim" or other nicknames associated with Barbados, including "Bimshire". The origin is uncertain, but several theories exist. The National Cultural Foundation of Barbados says that "Bim" was a word commonly used by slaves, and that it derives from the Igbo term bém from bé mụ́ meaning "my home, kindred, kind";[23] the Igbo phoneme [e] in the Igbo orthography is very close to /ɪ/.[24] The name could have arisen due to the relatively large percentage of Igbo slaves from modern-day southeastern Nigeria arriving in Barbados in the 18th century.[25][26] The words "Bim" and "Bimshire" are recorded in the Oxford English Dictionary and Chambers Twentieth Century Dictionaries. Another possible source for "Bim" is reported to be in the Agricultural Reporter of 25 April 1868, where the Rev. N. Greenidge (father of one of the island's most famous scholars, Abel Hendy Jones Greenidge) suggested that Bimshire was "introduced by an old planter listing it as a county of England". Expressly named were "Wiltshire, Hampshire, Berkshire and Bimshire".[23] Lastly, in the Daily Argosy (of Demerara, i.e. Guyana) of 1652, there is a reference to Bim as a possible corruption of "Byam", the name of a Royalist leader against the Parliamentarians. That source suggested the followers of Byam became known as "Bims" and that this became a word for all Barbadians.[23]

Historyedit
Main article: History of Barbados
Geological historyedit

Around 700,000 years ago, the island emerged from the ocean as a body of soft rock known as a diapir rose from the mantle beneath its present-day location. This process is still ongoing, raising Barbados at an average rate of 30 centimetres per thousand years.[27] Dozens of inland sea reefs still dominate coastal features within terraces and cliffs on the island.[27]

Pre-colonial periodedit

Archeological evidence suggests humans may have first settled or visited the island c. 1600 BC.[28][29][30] More permanent Amerindian settlement of Barbados dates to about the 4th to 7th centuries AD, by a group known as the Saladoid-Barrancoid.[31] Settlements of Arawaks from South America appeared by around 800 AD and again in the 12th–13th century.[28] The Kalinago (called "Caribs" by the Spanish) visited the island regularly, although there is no evidence of permanent settlement.[32]

European arrivaledit
Spanish map of the island (1632)

The first Europeans arrived at some time in the 15th or 16th century, but it is uncertain which European nation this was. One lesser-known source points to earlier revealed[clarification needed] works antedating contemporary sources, indicating it could have been the Spanish.[8] Many, if not most, believe it was the Portuguese, en route to Brazil.[33][34] The island was largely ignored by Europeans, though Spanish slave raiding is thought to have reduced the native population, with many fleeing to other islands.[28][35]

English settlement in the 17th centuryedit
George Washington House was visited by George Washington in 1751, in what is believed to have been his only trip outside the present-day United States.[36]

The first English ship, which had arrived on 14 May 1625, was captained by John Powell. The first settlement began on 17 February 1627, near what is now Holetown (formerly Jamestown, after King James I of England),[37] by a group led by John Powell's younger brother, Henry, consisting of 80 settlers and 10 English indentured labourers.[38] Some sources state that some Africans were among these first settlers.[28]

The settlement was established as a proprietary colony and funded by Sir William Courten, a City of London merchant who acquired the title to Barbados and several other islands. The first colonists were actually tenants, and much of the profits of their labour returned to Courten and his company.[39] Courten's title was later transferred to James Hay, 1st Earl of Carlisle, in what was called the "Great Barbados Robbery".[40] Carlisle then chose as governor Henry Powell, who established the House of Assembly in 1639, in an effort to appease the planters, who might otherwise have opposed his controversial appointment.[28][41]

English tobacco planters and slaves in Barbados, 17th century

In the period 1640–1660, the West Indies attracted more than two-thirds of the total number of English emigrants to the Americas. By 1650, there were 44,000 settlers in the West Indies, as compared to 12,000 on the Chesapeake and 23,000 in New England. Most English arrivals were indentured. After five years of labour, they were given "freedom dues" of about £10, usually in goods. Before the mid-1630s, they also received 5 to 10 acres (2 to 4 hectares) of land, but after that time the island filled and there was no more free land. During the Cromwellian era (1650s) this included a large number of prisoners-of-war, vagrants and people who were illicitly kidnapped, who were forcibly transported to the island and sold as servants. These last two groups were predominantly Irish, as several thousand were infamously rounded up by English merchants and sold into servitude in Barbados and other Caribbean islands during this period, a practice that came to be known as being Barbadosed.[41][42] Cultivation of sugar was thus handled primarily by European indentured labour until it became difficult to bring more indentured servants from England.[43]

Parish registers from the 1650s show that, for the white population, there were four times as many deaths as marriages. The mainstay of the infant colony's economy was the growth export of tobacco, but tobacco prices eventually fell in the 1630s as Chesapeake production expanded.[41]

Effects of the English Civil Waredit
Main articles: English overseas possessions in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms and Restoration in the English colonies

Around the same time, fighting during the War of the Three Kingdoms and the Interregnum spilled over into Barbados and Barbadian territorial waters. The island was not involved in the war until after the execution of Charles I, when the island's government fell under the control of Royalists (ironically the Governor, Philip Bell, remaining loyal to Parliament while the Barbadian House of Assembly, under the influence of Humphrey Walrond, supported Charles II). To try to bring the recalcitrant colony to heel, the Commonwealth Parliament passed an act on 3 October 1650 prohibiting trade between England and Barbados, and because the island also traded with the Netherlands, further Navigation Acts were passed, prohibiting any but English vessels trading with Dutch colonies. These acts were a precursor to the First Anglo-Dutch War. The Commonwealth of England sent an invasion force under the command of Sir George Ayscue, which arrived in October 1651. Ayscue, with a smaller force that included Scottish prisoners, surprised a larger force of Royalists, but had to resort to spying and diplomacy ultimately. On 11 January 1652, the Royalists in the House of Assembly led by Lord Willoughby surrendered, which marked the end of royalist privateering as a major threat.[44] The conditions of the surrender were incorporated into the Charter of Barbados (Treaty of Oistins), which was signed at the Mermaid's Inn, Oistins, on 17 January 1652.[45][46]

Irish people in Barbadosedit
Main article: Irish people in Barbados

Starting with Cromwell, a large percentage of the white labourer population were indentured servants and involuntarily transported people from Ireland. Irish servants in Barbados were often treated poorly, and Barbadian planters gained a reputation for cruelty.[47]: 55  The decreased appeal of an indenture on Barbados, combined with enormous demand for labour caused by sugar cultivation, led to the use of involuntary transportation to Barbados as a punishment for crimes, or for political prisoners, and also to the kidnapping of labourers who were deported to Barbados.[47]: 55  Irish indentured servants were a significant portion of the population throughout the period when white servants were used for plantation labour in Barbados, and while a "steady stream" of Irish servants entered Barbados throughout the 17th century, Cromwellian efforts to pacify Ireland created a "veritable tidal wave" of Irish labourers who were sent to Barbados during the 1650s.[47]: 56  Due to inadequate historical records, the total number of Irish labourers sent to Barbados is unknown, and estimates have been "highly contentious".[47]: 56  One historical source estimated that as many as 50,000 Irish people were deported to either Barbados or Virginia during the 1650s. Another estimate that 12,000 Irish prisoners had arrived in Barbados by 1655 has been described by historian Richard B. Sheridan.[48]: 236  According to historian Thomas Bartlett, it is "generally accepted" that approximately 10,000 Irish were deported to the West Indies and approximately 40,000 came as voluntary indentured servants, while many also travelled as voluntary, un-indentured emigrants.[49]: 256 

The sugar revolutionedit
Sunday market in Barbados during the colonial era
See also: Indian slave trade between Barbados and South Carolina

The introduction of sugar cane from Dutch Brazil in 1640[50] completely transformed society, the economy and the physical landscape.[51] Barbados eventually had one of the world's biggest sugar industries.[52] One group instrumental in ensuring the early success of the industry was the Sephardic Jews, who had originally been expelled from the Iberian peninsula, to end up in Dutch Brazil.[52] As the effects of the new crop increased, so did the shift in the ethnic composition of Barbados and surrounding islands.[41] The workable sugar plantation required a large investment and a great deal of heavy labour. At first, Dutch traders supplied the equipment, financing, and African slaves, in addition to transporting most of the sugar to Europe.[41][28] In 1644, the population of Barbados was estimated at 30,000, of whom about 800 were of African ancestry, with the remainder mainly of English ancestry. These English smallholders were eventually bought out, and the island filled up with large sugar plantations worked by African slaves.[28] By 1660 there was near parity, with 27,000 Black people and 26,000 White people. By 1666, at least 12,000 white smallholders had been bought out, died, or left the island, many choosing to emigrate to Jamaica or the American Colonies (notably the Carolinas).[28] As a result, Barbados enacted a slave code as a way of legislatively controlling its enslaved Black population.[53] The law's text was influential in laws in other colonies.[54]

By 1680 there were 20,000 free whites and 46,000 enslaved Africans;[28] by 1724, there were 18,000 free whites and 55,000 enslaved Africans.[41]

18th and 19th centuriesedit
Statue of Bussa, Bridgetown. Bussa led the largest slave rebellion in Barbadian history.

The harsh conditions endured by the slaves resulted in several planned slave rebellions, the largest of which was Bussa's rebellion in 1816 which was rapidly suppressed by the colonial authorities.[28] In 1819, another slave revolt broke out on Easter Day. The revolt was put down in blood, with heads being displayed on stakes. Nevertheless, the brutality of the repression shocked even England and strengthened the abolitionist movement.[55] Growing opposition to slavery led to its abolition in the British Empire in 1833.[28] The plantocracy class retained control of political and economic power on the island, with most workers living in relative poverty.[28]

The 1780 hurricane killed more than 4,000 people on Barbados.[56][57] In 1854, a cholera epidemic killed more than 20,000 inhabitants.[58]

20th century before independenceedit

Deep dissatisfaction with the situation on Barbados led many to emigrate.[28][59] Things came to a head in the 1930s during the Great Depression, as Barbadians began demanding better conditions for workers, the legalisation of trade unions and a widening of the franchise, which at that point was limited to male property owners.[28] As a result of the increasing unrest the British sent a commission, called the West Indies Royal Commission, or Moyne Commission, in 1938, which recommended enacting many of the requested reforms on the islands.[28] As a result, Afro-Barbadians began to play a much more prominent role in the colony's politics, with universal suffrage being introduced in 1950.[28]

Broad Street, Bridgetown in 1914

Prominent among these early activists was Grantley Herbert Adams, who helped found the Barbados Labour Party (BLP) in 1938.[60] He became the first Premier of Barbados in 1953, followed by fellow BLP-founder Hugh Gordon Cummins from 1958 to 1961. A group of left-leaning politicians who advocated swifter moves to independence broke off from the BLP and founded the Democratic Labour Party (DLP) in 1955.[61][62] The DLP subsequently won the 1961 Barbadian general election and their leader Errol Barrow became premier.[citation needed]

Full internal self-government was enacted in 1961.[28] Barbados joined the short-lived British West Indies Federation from 1958 to 1962, later gaining full independence on 30 November 1966.[28] Errol Barrow became the country's first prime minister.

Barbados opted to remain within the Commonwealth of Nations. Elizabeth II became Queen of Barbados and was represented locally by a governor-general.[63].

Post-independence eraedit

The Barrow government sought to diversify the economy away from agriculture, seeking to boost industry and the tourism sector. Barbados was also at the forefront of regional integration efforts, spearheading the creation of CARIFTA and CARICOM.[28] The DLP lost the 1976 Barbadian general election to the BLP under Tom Adams. Adams adopted a more conservative and strongly pro-Western stance, allowing the Americans to use Barbados as the launchpad for their invasion of Grenada in 1983.[64] Adams died in office in 1985 and was replaced by Harold Bernard St. John; however, St. John lost the 1986 Barbadian general election, which saw the return of the DLP under Errol Barrow, who had been highly critical of the US intervention in Grenada. Barrow, too, died in office, and was replaced by Lloyd Erskine Sandiford, who remained Prime Minister until 1994.[citation needed]

Owen Arthur of the BLP won the 1994 Barbadian general election, remaining prime minister until 2008.[65] Arthur was a strong advocate of republicanism, though a planned referendum to replace Queen Elizabeth as Head of State in 2008 never took place.[66] The DLP won the 2008 Barbadian general election, but the new Prime Minister David Thompson died in 2010 and was replaced by Freundel Stuart. The BLP returned to power in 2018 under Mia Mottley, who became Barbados's first female prime minister.[67]

Transition to republicedit
Main article: Republicanism in Barbados

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Communications in Barbados](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Communications_in_Barbados&redirect=no "Communications in Barbados"))

**Communications in Barbados** refers to the telephony, internet, postal, radio, and television systems of [Barbados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbados "Barbados"). [Barbados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbados "Barbados") has long been an informational and communications centre in the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean") region. [Electricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity "Electricity") coverage throughout Barbados is good and reliable. Usage is high and provided by a service monopoly, [Barbados Light & Power Company Ltd.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbados_Light_&_Power_Company_Ltd. "Barbados Light & Power Company Ltd.") (a division of [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada")-based [Emera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emera "Emera")).

The [International Telecommunication Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Telecommunication_Union "International Telecommunication Union") (ITU) [call sign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_sign "Call sign")[prefix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITU_prefix "ITU prefix") allocated for all [radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_station "Radio station") and [television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_station "Television station") broadcasts in Barbados is **8P**, and this replaced the former **ZN** and **VP6** as a [British territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telecommunications_in_Barbados&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [Cable and Wireless (Caribbean)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_and_Wireless_(Caribbean) "Cable and Wireless (Caribbean)")

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/All_Red_Line.jpg/250px-All_Red_Line.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:All_Red_Line.jpg)

The [All Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Red_Line "All Red Line") cable for the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"). Barbados(Barbadoes) functioned as an interconnection-point between [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda "Bermuda") and [Ascension Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascension_Island "Ascension Island") in the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"). c.a. 1903

Barbados has had various forms of Communications as early as the 1840s. Some of the earliest expressions of inter-island communication includes a number of signal stations built along the high points of the island to relay acts of transgression towards the island to the [Saint Ann's Garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Ann's_Garrison "Saint Ann's Garrison") on the south-west coast. The first telephone network in the country was developed in 1884.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_in_Barbados#cite_note-1) As the former [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire")'s [All Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Red_Line "All Red Line") came into existence during the early 1900s, Barbados played an important role as a crucial link in the [trans-Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") communications network. By 1935 a hard wired cable-based radio network was later deployed throughout the country to broadcast the [Rediffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rediffusion "Rediffusion") service directly from [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") to homes and business across Barbados.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_in_Barbados#cite_note-2) In 2001 the [Government of Barbados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Barbados "Government of Barbados") and the local [Incumbent Local Exchange Carrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incumbent_Local_Exchange_Carrier "Incumbent Local Exchange Carrier") (ILEC) provider, [Cable & Wireless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_and_Wireless_(Caribbean) "Cable and Wireless (Caribbean)") signed a MOU beginning a phased process of liberalisation of the international segment of Barbados' telecommunications sector.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_in_Barbados#cite_note-3) The process was aimed at bringing Barbados' sector into compliance with the [World Trade Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Organization "World Trade Organization") (WTO). The plan outlined the first phase commencing on 1 December 2001 and the entire process ending with full liberalisation being achieved on 1 August 2003. As these target dates were missed, the Phase I process was later commenced on 1 November 2002, with Phase II and III beginning on 16 November 2003 and 21 February 2004 respectively. Full liberalisation was attained in February, 2005, for the international telecommunications services market.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_in_Barbados#cite_note-4)

## Telephone

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telecommunications_in_Barbados&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Telephone")]

**[Country Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_calling_code "Country calling code"): [+1.246](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_code_246 "Area code 246")**  
**[International Call Prefix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Call_Prefix "International Call Prefix"): 011**[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_in_Barbados#cite_note-5) (outside NANP)

Calls from Barbados to the US, Canada, and other NANP Caribbean nations, are dialled as 1 + NANP area code + 7-digit number. Calls from Barbados to non-NANP countries are dialled as 011 + country code + phone number with local area code.

[**Number Format**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Numbering_Plan#Dialing_procedures "North American Numbering Plan"): nxx-xxxx

The rate of telecommunications penetration in Barbados ranks among the highest in the world. According to the [International Telecommunication Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Telecommunication_Union "International Telecommunication Union"), telephone service for the period 2000–2004, stated Barbados had 124 telephones in usage for every 100 people.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_in_Barbados#cite_note-6) Telecommunications are virtually universally accessible to all.

## Broadcasting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Telecommunications_in_Barbados&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Broadcasting")]

## FAQs

* * *

### What are the Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3 storage sizes?

 Meta Quest 3S will be available in two storage options: 128GB and 256GB.* 

 Meta Quest 3 is available in two storage options: 128GB while supplies last, and 512GB.* 

 *Available storage is less than shown due to existing software. Meta Quest 3 will require certain updates to be installed from time to time, including prior to first use. 

* * *

### Is Meta Quest 3S lighter than Meta Quest 3?

 They are close to the same weight. Meta Quest 3S (513 grams) is approximately 2 grams lighter than Meta Quest 3 (515 grams)—roughly equal to a small metal paper clip or pen cap. 

* * *

### Are Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3 wireless?

 Yes, Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3 are both all-in-one wireless headsets. 

* * *

### Do I need a Facebook account for Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3?

 No, you don’t need a Facebook account to use Meta Quest 3S or Meta Quest 3. You just need a Meta account which you can create with an email address, if you don’t already have one. 

* * *

### Can Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3 play Steam games?

 Yes, you can stream the games you love in your Steam library from your computer to both Meta Quest headsets via [Steamlink](https://l.facebook.com/experiences/steam-link/5841245619310585/). 

* * *

### What can you use Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3 for?

[Gaming](https://l.facebook.com/quest/gaming/)  
 The biggest titles on the biggest screens. Play your favorite titles on giant 2D screens, or dive into fully immersive action and step into the shoes of your favorite characters. 

[Entertainment](https://l.facebook.com/quest/entertainment/)  
 Have your own personal theater at home or on the go with Travel Mode. Stream your favorite shows while keeping all your surroundings in view and adjust the screen for size and placement. 

[Social experiences](https://l.facebook.com/quest/social/)  
 With Quest, you can enjoy popular social apps and multiplayer games, connect with friends from anywhere, host a meeting with colleagues in Meta Horizon Workrooms and more. 

[Fitness](https://l.facebook.com/quest/fitness/)  
 Invite a personal trainer into your living room or travel to stunning locations for unreal workouts, with a totally wireless experience. 

* * *

### Do you need a computer for Meta Quest 3S or Meta Quest 3?

 No, just download the Meta Horizon App to your smartphone, then wirelessly connect your headset and smartphone to complete the setup process. You can shop top virtual reality titles from the mobile app, or while you’re in the headset. 

Get the app

[![Image 24](https://lookaside.fbsbx.com/elementpath/media/?media_id=1245599749278684&version=1776419943&transcode_extension=webp)](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.oculus.twilight)

[![Image 25](https://lookaside.fbsbx.com/elementpath/media/?media_id=202442761988127&version=1776419943&transcode_extension=webp)](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/oculus-vr/id1366478176)

* * *

### How long is the battery life of Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3?

 The Meta Quest 3S battery lasts up to 2.5 hours of usage on average.* The Meta Quest 3 battery lasts up to 2.2 hours of usage on average.* 

 You can get up to 2 additional hours of headset time and added comfort with the [Meta Quest 3 Elite Strap with Battery](https://www.meta.com/quest/accessories/elite-strap-battery/?utm_source=www.meta.com&utm_medium=organicsearch) accessory. 

 *As with most battery powered devices, battery life is dependent on various factors such as device settings, usage, age of battery, Bluetooth usage, and wireless conditions. 

* * *

### Can you watch movies on Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3?

 Yes, with our recently announced Theater Mode you can turn anywhere into your own theater with Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3. Whether you're in your house or on the go, start your movie and watch the room around you automatically darken. Anchor your screen to the perfect placement, and then kick back and enjoy the show. Movie content is available from Netflix and more. 

* * *

### Can you wear glasses with Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3?

 Yes. You can wear glasses with the Meta Quest 3S using the glasses spacer included in the box. Custom prescription Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3 lenses are available for added comfort (sold separately). 

* * *

### What is the difference between Meta Quest 3S and Meta Quest 3?

 The Meta Quest 3S offers unreal experiences at an unreal price that invites even more people to dive in. 
*    Meta Quest 3S storage options: 128GB at $349.99, and 256GB* at $449.99
*    Meta Quest 3S optics quality: High-definition resolution with 1832x1920 pixels per eye 
*    Meta Quest headset design: Lightweight comfort 

 The Meta Quest 3 is our most ultimate Meta Quest experience, with next-level performance** and life-like visuals. 
*    Meta Quest 3 storage options: 512GB* at $599.99
*    Meta Quest 3 optics quality: 4K+ Infinite Display, 30% more pixels 
*    Meta Quest headset design: Premium slim comfort 

 **Available storage is less than shown due to existing software. Meta Quest 3 will require certain updates to be installed from time to time, including prior to first use. 

 **Based on the graphic performance of the Qualcomm Snapdragon XR2 Gen 2 platform vs the Meta Quest 2 platform.

Day 1: The Divide – From Suspicion to Synergy in Zimbabwean Football To bridge the gap between Zimbabwe’s diaspora talent and our local football structures, we must first understand its origins. The journey from suspicion to synergy requires a crucial mindset shift. The chasm wasn't created overnight. It was carved by isolated incidents, systemic inertia, and a fundamental clash of perspectives. The Two Sides of the Divide: · The Local Viewpoint: Diaspora players are sometimes viewed with suspicion—seen as privileged, "difficult to manage," or lacking the commitment of those developed in the local system. Past scandals have framed their engagement as a transactional risk. · The Diaspora Viewpoint: Engaging with Zimbabwean football can feel like navigating a labyrinth. The lack of professional structures, consistent communication, and long-term planning is frustrating for those accustomed to organized environments. The central question is one of trust. This mutual misunderstanding is our greatest barrier, perpetuating a false division between "local" and "import." The Mindset Shift: From Gatekeeping to Stewardship The transformation we need is foundational. We must move: · From Threat to Tide: Diaspora talent isn't taking a spot from a local player; it's raising the level of competition, introducing new techniques, and expanding the footballing IQ of the entire squad. · From Transaction to Investment: It’s not just about capping a player for one tournament. It’s about a long-term investment in our national football ecosystem by integrating their knowledge, discipline, and networks. · From Ad-Hoc to Proactive: We must move beyond last-minute calls and build a transparent, welcoming pathway for any Zimbabwean, anywhere, to contribute. The divide was built on outdated notions. Our future depends on our ability to dismantle them and embrace a new, inclusive philosophy. Africa’s Rise in Football Ownership: Redefining Global Power in the Game A quiet revolution is taking place across European football. African investors — from Egypt’s Nassef Sawiris (co-owner of Aston Villa) to Nigeria’s Kunle Soname and Nneka Ede — are reshaping the ownership landscape of the sport. This shift marks a new era where African capital, talent, and leadership are no longer confined to the pitch — they are shaping boardrooms, strategies, and international partnerships. Unlike the speculative takeovers of the past, these investments are rooted in strategic development: infrastructure growth, youth academies, and cross-continental pathways between African and European clubs. It’s a bridge between two football ecosystems that share talent but are now starting to share ownership and opportunity as well. From a business perspective, this movement represents diversification and the democratization of global sport. From a cultural standpoint, it’s about representation — showing that leadership in football can emerge from any part of the world when vision meets investment. The future of football will not be shaped by geography, but by who builds with purpose. ⚽️ Bridging Worlds: Uniting Diaspora Talent with Zimbabwean Football For decades, Zimbabwean football has been a story of unrealized potential. A silent divide exists between those shaping the game at home and the vast, underutilized resource of our diaspora that is players, coaches, medics, analysts, and administrators. This series, “Bridging Worlds,” seeks to change that. It’s a call to reimagine our football by merging the raw passion of our grassroots with the expertise and exposure of Zimbabweans abroad. This isn't just about players with foreign passports; it's about building an inclusive ecosystem where being Zimbabwean isn't bound by geography. Globally, nations like Morocco and Cape Verde have shown that integrating diaspora talent is a strategic advantage. Their success hinges on systems of collaboration, not isolation. For Zimbabwe, the challenge is both cultural and structural, from overcoming past mistrust to building a national philosophy that welcomes all who can contribute, whether they are in Bulawayo or Birmingham. Over this series, we will explore: 1️⃣The origins of the diaspora-local divide. 2️⃣Lessons from nations that mastered integration. 3️⃣️Tapping into the full spectrum of diaspora expertise. 4️⃣️Proposing governance frameworks for trust & accountability. 5️⃣️A vision for a unified Zimbabwe Global Football Network. If our football is to reclaim its identity, we must do more than produce talent—we must connect our people. The dream begins with a simple truth: we are stronger together. ⚽ Governance: The Bedrock for Rebuilding Zimbabwean Football We’ve established that integrating diaspora talent is a strategic imperative for Zimbabwean football. But how do we move from vision to reality? The answer lies in one word: Governance. Past mistrust, like the infamous "passport scandal," stems from a structural failure: the lack of transparent, accountable frameworks for engagement. We cannot rely on patchwork solutions. A complete rebuild is needed, grounded in three pillars: 1. Institutional Transparency – Restoring Trust Trust is the currency of collaboration,and in Zimbabwean football, it has been devalued. Rebuilding it requires: · Standardized Contracts: Clear, transparent agreements for match fees, bonuses, and reimbursements. · A Diaspora Liaison Desk: A professional, single point of contact for all logistical and contractual matters. · Public Accountability: Independent auditing and public reporting of development funds from FIFA, CAF, or government. 2. Diaspora Inclusion – From Guests to Partners Diaspora professionals must be architects of the system,not temporary guests. This requires: · A Global Football Advisory Board (GFAB): A formal board of diaspora experts to advise on strategy and policy. · Representation in Technical Roles: Strategic appointments of qualified diaspora coaches, scouts, and analysts. · A Global Scouting Network: A standardized, data-driven system to identify and evaluate talent across all diaspora hubs. 3. Performance Accountability – Measuring What Matters Governance is empty without measurable outcomes.We must adopt: · A National Football Philosophy: A long-term mandate that integrates diaspora participation into all pathways. · An Annual Integration Scorecard: A public report tracking metrics like diaspora coach engagement and player integrations. · Mandatory Professional Development: Continuous upskilling of local staff by diaspora experts to align with global standards. The Bottom Line Bridging the diaspora-local divide is a governance [challenge.By](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=http%3A%2F%2Fchallenge%2EBy&urlhash=2I30&trk=public_post-text) institutionalizing transparency, embedding diaspora expertise, and enforcing accountability, we can evolve from a fragmented ecosystem into a unified, professional network. This is the hard work of reconstruction, rebuilding trust, restoring standards, and renewing purpose. CAF's Success Under Motsepe: The Confederation of African Football(CAF) returned to profitability under Patrice Motsepe due to a focus on transparency, aggressive commercial growth, and strategic leadership. By restoring credibility, attracting new sponsors, and reinvesting in competitions, Motsepe demonstrated that good governance is the foundation for financial success in sports. Blueprint for Kenya: For Kenya to emulate this success and build a profitable sports sector,it must: 1. Enact Root-and-Branch Governance Reform: Overhaul the Football Kenya Federation (FKF) with a competent, transparent, and accountable leadership team. 2. Attract Business Minds: Involve Kenyan business leaders and investors for their strategic acumen and to foster public-private partnerships. 3. Monetize the Product: Professionally rebrand and market the league, bundle broadcasting rights for higher value, and secure major local corporate sponsorships. 4. Invest in Infrastructure: Use partnerships to build modern stadiums and reinvest profits into youth development for long-term sustainability. Conclusion: The core lesson from CAF is that Kenya's sports potential is held back not by a lack of resources,but by a lack of trust and competence. By prioritizing professional, business-like management and transparency, Kenya can unlock its massive sporting potential.

**MTN Group Limited** (formerly **M-Cell**)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-2) is a [South African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa")[multinational corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation") and mobile [telecommunications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecommunications "Telecommunications") provider. Its head office is in [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-4) MTN is among the [largest mobile network operators in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mobile_network_operators "List of mobile network operators"), and the largest in [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa").

In October 2025, MTN announced it had surpassed 300 million customers, the first African-headquartered telco to reach that milestone, making it the sixth-largest in the world by subscriber count. It has a footprint in sixteen countries in Africa and the Middle East.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The company was founded in 1994 as M-Cell with assistance from the South African government.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-8) In 1995, it replaced its then CEO, John Beck, with Robert (Bob) Chaphe and founder Leena Jaitley.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-9) In 2001, the company reported that its controlling shareholder was Johnnic Holdings, and the chairperson was [Irene Charnley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_Charnley "Irene Charnley").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-10) In 2002, [Phuthuma Nhleko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phuthuma_Nhleko "Phuthuma Nhleko") became the CEO,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-11) replacing then-CEO Paul Edwards, who had invested in expansion to Nigeria.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-12) MTN's competitors in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") include [Vodacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vodacom "Vodacom"), [Cell C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_C "Cell C") and [Telkom Mobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telkom_Mobile "Telkom Mobile").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-13)

In May 2008, [Bharti Airtel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharti_Airtel "Bharti Airtel"), an India-based telecommunications company, explored the possibility of buying MTN Group.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-14)[Reliance Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reliance_Communications "Reliance Communications") was also in talks with MTN for a "potential combination of their businesses".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-16) In July, the two companies ended discussions regarding the merger.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-17) In June 2008, MTN Group agreed to purchase Verizon Business South Africa, which was a provider of data services to customers in South Africa and four other African countries.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-18) The acquisition was completed on 28 February 2009.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-19) On 26 June 2009, MTN Group's subsidiary merged with [Belgacom International Carrier Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BICS_(company) "BICS (company)") (BICS), a subsidiary of [Belgacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgacom "Belgacom").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-21) The combined subsidiary functioned as the international gateway for carrier services of MTN.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-22)

In October 2012, MTN announced a partnership with [Afrihost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrihost "Afrihost") to provide [DSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_subscriber_line "Digital subscriber line") Broadband services in Africa.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-24) In November 2012, South African [holding company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holding_company "Holding company")[Shanduka Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanduka_Group "Shanduka Group") acquired a minority stake in MTN Group's Nigeria business for $335 million.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-25)

In 2014, the company sold its [tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_masts_and_towers "Radio masts and towers") portfolios in [Côte d'Ivoire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B4te_d'Ivoire "Côte d'Ivoire"), [Cameroon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameroon "Cameroon"), [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") and [Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda") to [IHS Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IHS_Towers "IHS Towers").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-26) That year, MTN was named to the 2014 BrandZ Top 100 Most Valuable Global Brand rankings and named the Most Admired and Most Valuable Brand in Africa,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-:0-27) retaining the latter ranking in 2015.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-:0-27) IHS Towers later acquired MTN South Africa's towers, in 2022.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-28) In March 2016, the company appointed Rob Shuter as [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer"),[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-29) who was succeeded on 1 September 2020 by [Ralph Mupita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Mupita "Ralph Mupita").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-30)

In May 2023, in support of the company's "Ambition 2025" plan to structurally separate its fibre business; MTN rebranded subsidiary MTN GlobalConnect as Bayobab, operating as Bayobab Fibre and Bayobab Communication.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-31) On March 14, 2024, several undersea cables were cut, disrupting service for the Africa Coast to Europe.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-32) Bayobab repaired the disabled ACE and WASC lines during the following week.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-33)

### MTN Ghana IPO

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: MTN Ghana IPO")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Sim_Card_Registration_by_MTN_Ghana.jpg/250px-Sim_Card_Registration_by_MTN_Ghana.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sim_Card_Registration_by_MTN_Ghana.jpg)

MTN Sim Card re-registration in [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra"), [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana "Ghana")

On 31 May 2018, MTN Ghana launched its initial public offering (IPO).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-41) The IPO closed on 31 July 2019. A total of up to 4,637,394,533 ordinary shares of MTN Ghana, representing 35% of its equity was offered to qualifying applicants. This was part of the agreement between MTN Ghana and Ghana's [National Communications Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Communications_Authority "National Communications Authority") (NCA) in November, 2015 for MTN Ghana to deploy 4G LTE mobile services to its customers in Ghana.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-42) Among other methods of payments, MTN [mobile money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_MobileMoney "African MobileMoney") was included as a payment option for the MTN share offer subscription. This was the first time mobile money had been used as a payment method in an IPO.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-43) In December 2024, MTN appointed Stephen Blewett as CEO of MTN Ghana, succeeding [Selorm Adadevoh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selorm_Adadevoh "Selorm Adadevoh"), who moved to the position of Group Chief Commercial Officer. Blewett assumed the role on 1 April 2025.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-44)

### MTN Shuts Down Stores

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: MTN Shuts Down Stores")]

On 23 February 2017, Nigerian protestors attacked a MTN office in [Abuja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abuja "Abuja"), [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria "Nigeria") as a counterattack due to violence targeted against Nigerians in South Africa.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-46)

In September 2019 MTN began closing stores in Nigeria and some of their stores in [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg"), [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") due to rioting, looting, and attacks on some of their facilities.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-52)

[Geoffrey Onyeama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Onyeama "Geoffrey Onyeama") the Nigerian Foreign Minister stated at a press briefing on 4 September 2019, that MTN group along with Shoprite, stated that the targeted South African stores in Nigeria are "subsidiaries that are owned by Nigerians." And that "the property owned by Nigerians within Nigeria and the people working there are Nigerians."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-53)

[Lai Mohammed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lai_Mohammed "Lai Mohammed"), Nigeria's Minister of Information and Culture, reported that some of the South African companies that were attacked in Nigeria have Nigerian investors owning significant amounts of stakes, and Nigerian employees.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-55)

MTN has stated that they will continue to do business in Nigeria.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-57)

### Services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Services")]

In March 2019 MTN launched a [WhatsApp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WhatsApp "WhatsApp") channel to let its customers buy airtime and data bundles through the messaging app.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-:1-58) Customers can also check their balances and store their credit or [debit cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debit_card "Debit card") in the app for future purchases. The service is provided by another South African company, Clickatell.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-:1-58)

In the same year, MTN launched a communication platform [ayoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayoba_(company) "Ayoba (company)").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-59)

### Cyprus branch re-branding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Cyprus branch re-branding")]

MTN sold its [Cyprus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus "Cyprus") branch to [Monaco Telecom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco_Telecom "Monaco Telecom") for €260 million in July 2018.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-60) It was later re-branded as Epic in June 2019.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-62) In December 2019, former Deputy Finance Minister of the [Government of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_South_Africa "Government of South Africa"), [Mcebisi Jonas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mcebisi_Jonas "Mcebisi Jonas"), was appointed as the board chairperson of the company.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-63)

### Middle East exodus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Middle East exodus")]

In August 2020, MTN decided to sell its shares in [Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria "Syria"), [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan "Afghanistan") and [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen "Yemen"), and to divest its 49% minority holding in [Irancell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irancell "Irancell") over time. The company's decision was based on the fact that their assets in the Middle East contributed less than 4% to group earnings in the first half of the year.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-64) MTN Group has transferred its majority 82.8% shareholding in MTN Yemen to Emerald International Investment, thereby exiting the market.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-65)

### Sale of stake in Jumia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Sale of stake in Jumia")]

On 30 October 2020, MTN made public the sale of their shares in the e-commerce brand [Jumia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jumia "Jumia"). The sale was worth US$142.31 million dollars.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-66)

### MTN Mastercard Collaboration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: MTN Mastercard Collaboration")]

In February 2021, the MTN Group partnered with [Mastercard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastercard "Mastercard") to ensure safe and secure global e-commerce payments of their customer base in 16 African countries. A Mastercard virtual payment platform, that is linked to MTN MoMo (Mobile Money) wallets makes this possible.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-67)

### Mobile Money spin-off

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=MTN_Group&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Mobile Money spin-off")]

In March 2021, MTN CEO [Ralph Mupita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Mupita "Ralph Mupita") announced during the company's annual results call that the group was now considering spinning off its mobile money activities. "We see a separation and carve out of our fintech business as something that we have to do".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-68) In April 2021, he estimated the value of the group's mobile money arm to at least US$5 to 6 billion.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_Group#cite_note-69)
